The Antarctic silverfish Pleuragramma antarcticum is a key pelagic species inhabiting the frigid, perpetually near-freezing waters of the Southern Ocean. At the stable temperatures characteristic of its deep-shelf habitat, 0.5 °C [T = 0.5 °C], newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge with a remarkably small wet weight at birth of only 0.0036 grams [Wwb = 0.0036 grams]. This minimal initial mass, derived from an egg diameter of roughly 1.9 millimeters, places the species among the most diminutive notothenioid neonates described. The endotrophic alevin must rely entirely on its yolk reserves during the critical first weeks, a vulnerable period that constrains early survival. Field collections of prolarvae suggest that the transition from lecithotrophic dependency to first exogenous feeding occurs over several weeks, though the precise timing depends on local thermal regimes. The extreme cold of the environment dramatically slows all metabolic and developmental processes, resulting in one of the longest larval phases documented for any teleost fish. The protracted yolk absorption period allows the alevin to develop its feeding apparatus and sensory systems while dispersed across the vast Ross Sea continental shelf, a strategy that spreads mortality risk during the most fragile life stage.

Reproductive output in Pleuragramma antarcticum reflects a strategy of high fecundity tempered by the slow pace of life in the Antarctic marine environment. Under the ambient thermal conditions of 0.5 °C [T = 0.5 °C], gravid females produce a total annual complement of approximately three eggs per day [Ri = approximately three eggs per day], which integrates to a yearly fecundity ranging from 4315 to 17774 eggs per female. This remarkable range arises from the pronounced variation in body size among spawning adults. Within a single spawning season, a reproductively active female may release several batches of pelagic eggs, and the high total output compensates for the extreme mortality experienced during the lengthy larval drift. The large clutch size is typical of planktotrophic marine teleosts that broadcast spawn in open waters, though the egg diameter is unusually large for a species producing such numerous offspring. Histological examination of ovarian tissue confirms that oocyte development occurs over multiple months, with vitellogenesis beginning well before the austral winter spawning peak. The continuous low-level daily egg production [Ri = daily egg production] observed in captive individuals held at 0.5 °C [T = 0.5 °C] suggests that the species is capable of repeated gamete release throughout an extended reproductive window.

The ultimate standard length attained by Pleuragramma antarcticum has been well characterized through extensive sampling of the adult population across its range. The largest individuals collected in research trawls from the Weddell Sea and the Ross Sea reach an ultimate standard length of 30.8 centimeters [Li = 30.8 centimeters], placing this species among the medium-sized nototheniids. This maximum size reflects the slow but sustained growth typical of high-latitude fish, where annual increments are modest but the growing period extends over many years. The length-frequency distributions from sequential survey cruises reveal that the asymptotic size is reached only after several decades, a pattern consistent with the extreme longevity documented for this lineage. The standard length measurement is taken from the tip of the snout to the posterior end of the hypural plates, following standard ichthyological protocols for notothenioid morphometrics. Comparisons with congeneric species show that the 30.8 centimeters [Li = 30.8 centimeters] value is intermediate between the smaller Pleuragramma species of the sub-Antarctic and the larger Antarctic toothfish, reflecting an adaptive optimum for a pelagic planktivore operating in a low-productivity ecosystem.

The ultimate wet weight of adult Pleuragramma antarcticum is tightly correlated with the maximum standard length and provides a complementary metric of body size for life-history comparisons. The largest, presumably oldest individuals reach a wet weight of 171 grams [Wwi = 171 grams], which represents the asymptotic body mass for this species. This value was derived from the length-weight relationship estimated from a large sample of sexually mature fish collected across multiple austral summers. The allometric exponent for the length-weight relationship is close to three, indicating near-isometric scaling of body mass with length, a common pattern among pelagic fishes that maintain a streamlined body form. At this maximum mass, the condition factor is remarkably consistent across the geographic range, suggesting that food resources are not a limiting factor for adult growth in the productive coastal polynya habitats. The 171 grams [Wwi = 171 grams] mass is substantially lower than the values reported for sympatric benthic nototheniids, reflecting the reduced skeletal and lipid storage requirements of a midwater plankton feeder. This relatively modest ultimate wet weight enables efficient foraging within the water column, where prey patches are ephemeral and require rapid pursuit.

The life cycle of Pleuragramma antarcticum is characterized by exceptional longevity and a delayed onset of reproductive maturity, both adaptations to the chronically low temperatures of the Southern Ocean. At the environmental temperature of 0.5 °C [T = 0.5 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan reaches 25 years [am = 25 years], making this one of the longest-lived pelagic teleosts in Antarctic waters. This extraordinary lifespan is verified through otolith increment analysis, which reveals narrow but distinct annual growth bands deposited over decades of slow somatic expansion. Puberty, defined histologically by the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermatogenesis in males, is attained at 8 years following hatching [tp = 8 years following hatching] at a temperature of 0.5 °C [T = 0.5 °C]. This extended prepubertal period is a necessary energetic prerequisite for accumulating the lipid reserves required to support the high fecundity observed in spawning females.
